verses.text: When Jerusalem was taken, (in the ninth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and all his army came against Jerusalem, and besieged it.
In the eleventh year of Zedekiah, in the fourth month, the ninth day of the month, a breach was made in the city),

all the princes of the king of Babylon came in, and sat in the middle gate, Nergal Sharezer, Samgarnebo, Sarsechim, Rabsaris, Nergal Sharezer, Rabmag, with all the rest of the princes of the king of Babylon.

When Zedekiah the king of Judah and all the men of war saw them, then they fled, and went out of the city by night, by the way of the king’s garden, through the gate between the two walls; and he went out toward the Arabah.

But the army of the Chaldeans pursued them, and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho: and when they had taken him, they brought him up to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon to Riblah in the land of Hamath; and he gave judgment on him.
Then the king of Babylon killed the sons of Zedekiah in Riblah before his eyes. The king of Babylon also killed all the nobles of Judah.
Moreover he put out Zedekiah’s eyes, and bound him in fetters, to carry him to Babylon.
The Chaldeans burned the king’s house, and the houses of the people, with fire, and broke down the walls of Jerusalem.

Then Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive into Babylon the residue of the people who remained in the city, the deserters also who fell away to him, and the residue of the people who remained.
But Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard left of the poor of the people, who had nothing, in the land of Judah, and gave them vineyards and fields at the same time.
Now Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon commanded Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard concerning Jeremiah, saying,
“Take him, and look well to him, and do him no harm; but do to him even as he shall tell you.”
So Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard sent, and Nebushazban, Rabsaris, and Nergal Sharezer, Rabmag, and all the chief officers of the king of Babylon;
they sent, and took Jeremiah out of the court of the guard, and committed him to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, that he should carry him home: so he lived among the people.
Now Yahweh’s word came to Jeremiah, while he was shut up in the court of the guard, saying,

“Go, and speak to Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, saying, Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says: ‘Behold, I will bring my words on this city for evil, and not for good; and they shall be accomplished before you in that day.
But I will deliver you in that day,’ says Yahweh; ‘and you will not be given into the hand of the men of whom you are afraid.
For I will surely save you, and you shall not fall by the sword, but your life shall be for a prey to you; because you have put your trust in me,’ says Yahweh.”

footnotes.content: Here it comes—the judgment so long warned through Jeremiah's voice. Jerusalem falls because she would not listen. Even in ruin, we see God's Word is not empty air but accomplishes what it says. The Lord warns us because He loves us, not because He enjoys the breaking.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The walls crack open—the very walls that once held the city safe. When we trust ourselves instead of the Lord, our defenses crumble. In that moment of breach, you learn whether your confidence rested on brick and mortar or on His mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Babylonian princes sit in the middle gate—the very heart of the city's government—and Jerusalem's fate passes to foreign hands. Yet even Babylon's authority is held by God. The gate that once decided the city's law now opens to the Lord's judgment. He is sovereign even over those who do not know His name.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zedekiah flees by night through the garden gate—shame and panic in the dark. He who would not listen to Jeremiah in the light now runs blind into ruin. When we refuse God's gentle word, we choose to stumble in the dark.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Caught in Jericho's plains—the very place where Israel once conquered in faith, now the king is captured in unbelief. What a bitter echo. The Lord does not forget His promises, but He will not overlook rebellion either.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sons killed before the father's eyes, nobles destroyed—the pain is complete. Yet even in this darkness, God is writing a story that does not end in death. Judgment falls, yes, but the Lord's mercy will outlast it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zedekiah's eyes are put out and he is bound. A king who would not see the truth now cannot see at all. His blindness is the wages of his choice—yet even blind, bound prisoners remain the Lord's concern.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: House after house burns; the walls come down. The city that refused the Lord's Word crumbles under the sword. It seems the end of everything. But God's Word does not burn, and His purpose stands when stone turns to ash.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people are carried away captive—women, children, the weak. Exile is bitter. Yet even in Babylon the Lord will not abandon His own. Joseph was a prisoner too, and the Lord was with him. Captivity is not the end of God's faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The poorest are left behind—given fields and vineyards. Even in ruin, the Lord provides. The very ones with nothing are gifted a living. In His judgment there is mercy, and in His winnowing He remembers the humble.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nebuchadnezzar himself commands: Jeremiah must be protected and honored. What a strange mercy—the pagan king treasures the prophet his own people wanted dead. The Lord moves the heart of the king like water in His hand, caring for His servant even in an enemy's court.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Do him no harm; do as he tells you." The man Judah despised is now protected by a foreign power. God honours His faithful prophets even when the nations do not. To stand for His Word is to stand on the rock that cannot be moved.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The chief officers of Babylon gather—not to harm, but to obey the king's protection of Jeremiah. When God wills it, even the mighty bend to guard His servants. No power on earth rises above His purposes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah is released to Gedaliah's care and lives among the people. From the guard's court to a home—this is God's way of saying, "Your faithfulness matters." The prophet goes free while the city lies in ashes. Truth-telling costs, but the truth-teller is vindicated.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even in the court of the guard, even while bound, the Word of the Lord comes to Jeremiah. Chains cannot stop the Spirit's voice. His message is not finished—judgment has fallen, but redemption still speaks.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ebedmelech the Ethiopian—a foreigner, a servant—becomes the Lord's messenger to. After witnessing judgment on the city, he hears it confirmed: the Lord's words come to pass. His faithfulness will be remembered before the throne of heaven.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I will deliver you in that day"—not because Ebedmelech is great, but because he trusted the Lord. The men he feared hold no real power over him. When we fear the Lord, no human threat can touch us where it matters most.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Your life shall be for a prey to you"—you will live and keep your life. Readers today hear an echo here: when we trust Jesus, our lives are secure in Him, held as His treasure. The threats that surrounded Ebedmelech pale beside the promise that the faithful are kept.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
